name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,505

clue.text: Just starting another nice pint - drunk? I must be!

indicators.note: something drunk is reeling and disordered, so the letters before it stagger into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the speaker joins the fodder, as the drinker who must be drunk

explanation.surface: A drinker on yet another pint wonders, tipsy, whether they are already drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'another' only smooths the surface; the anagram uses NICE PINT plus the closing I.
explanation.definitionFit: Incipient describes something in its first stage, beginning to happen or develop.

clue.text: How about this island? Grand present, eh!

blocks.note: I is the abbreviation for island
a grand is a thousand, written K
the present moment
both are ways of asking someone to repeat themselves

explanation.surface: Someone offers an island as a lavish gift, asking if that would do.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase introduces a sudden suggestion, much like saying 'here is an idea' before proposing something.

clue.text: Regret punching Conservative and Liberal, causing pain

indicators.note: a fist punching into something ends up inside it, so one word sits within the others

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
to rue is to regret
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A political grudge leads someone to lash out at two parties.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone cruel inflicts suffering deliberately, so the adjective and the phrase describe the same harmful behaviour.

clue.text: Dying of cold

blocks.note: first meaning: passing away
second meaning: bitterly chilly weather

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one phrase about hypothermia; British speakers call bitter weather perishing, which is the second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The participle means expiring, and in British usage the adjective means freezing, as in a perishing wind.

clue.text: Silent revolutionary holding small signs up

indicators.note: a revolutionary overturns the established order, so the neighbouring word has its letters turned about
to hold something is to keep it within, so one piece is clasped inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A quiet rebel is raising placards in protest.
explanation.walkthrough: S is the clothing-label abbreviation for small; it lands inside the rearranged letters, not at either end.
explanation.definitionFit: To enlist is to join up, especially for military service, which is putting your name forward or registering.

clue.text: Where hookers head to score crack and bit of coke

blocks.note: to have a crack at something is to try it
a line is a single dose of cocaine laid out for snorting

explanation.surface: Seedy picture of prostitutes going to buy drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby a hooker is a forward; players head for the line to score a try. The sleazy reading is pure misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: Rugby points for a try come from grounding the ball over this marked boundary, where all players, hookers included, aim.

clue.text: See you are demure interviewing odious Soviet leaders

indicators.note: leaders go in front, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: the initial letters of these five words

explanation.surface: A modest reporter questions some unpleasant Soviet politicians.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the Spanish farewell, used in English as a casual goodbye, just as people part with a breezy see you.

clue.text: A boxing match round

blocks.note: taken as written
a bout is a fight in the ring

explanation.surface: Describing a single round in a boxing contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' looks like the boxing term, but here it is a preposition: about the house, round the house.
explanation.definitionFit: As prepositions or adverbs both mean surrounding or in the vicinity, as in walking about or round the town.

clue.text: Clumsy jerk: GET IN LANE!

indicators.note: a sudden jerk throws things out of place, so the following letters get scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An exasperated driver shouts at a hopeless motorist to stay in lane.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inelegant lacks grace or polish, which is awkward and ungainly in manner.

clue.text: Break with first of snooker shots

indicators.note: first of points to the opening letter alone of the following word

blocks.note: to snap is to break suddenly
its opening letter

explanation.surface: A snooker player opens the frame with a break of shots.
explanation.walkthrough: The snooker setting suggests cue shots, but the definition means photographs.
explanation.definitionFit: Snaps are casual photographs, and photographers take shots, so both nouns mean quick pictures.

clue.text: In an inoffensive way, Earl breaks up crazy gathering

indicators.note: breaking up something means splitting it open, so a letter is wedged into its middle

blocks.note: a nut is a crazy person
E is the abbreviation for earl
a rally is a mass meeting

explanation.surface: A nobleman diplomatically breaks up a wild get-together.
explanation.definitionFit: To act neutrally is to take no side, giving no offence to anyone on either side.

clue.text: Love's great - The End

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis scoring, written O
mega is slang for great

explanation.surface: A romantic movie poster: love is wonderful, then the closing credit.
explanation.definitionFit: Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, hence a byword for the final part or conclusion.

clue.text: Wife and son drinking beer in country

indicators.note: whoever is drinking takes the drink inside, so one piece goes within the pair

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for wife
ale is a type of beer
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A family scene of mother and son having a pint in the countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: Wales is one of the four nations of the United Kingdom, west of England.

clue.text: Lazy way to cut down on changing gear?

definitions.text: way to cut down on changing gear

blocks.note: first meaning: idle and lacking ambition

blocks.clueFragment: way to cut down on changing gear
blocks.note: second, playful meaning: driving with fewer gear shifts

explanation.surface: A lazy driver's trick for avoiding the gearstick.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the word into two: fewer shifts, a shift being a gear change.
explanation.definitionFit: A shiftless person is idle and without drive, unwilling to make any effort or plans.

clue.text: Me and my flipping family must tuck into seconds

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the word is read backwards
to tuck into is to fit inside, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: my! and oh! are both exclamations of surprise
S is the abbreviation for second, doubled for the plural
kin are relatives

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that their wretched relatives are tucking into second helpings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Me' in a clue means the setter, and this puzzle is by Hoskins. 'flipping' looks like a mild curse.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoskins is the pseudonym of this puzzle's compiler, so the setter speaking of himself is that name.

clue.text: Tired and broken

blocks.note: first meaning: utterly exhausted, in British slang
second meaning: smashed to pieces

explanation.walkthrough: Shattered is everyday British slang for worn out, alongside its literal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means smashed into fragments, and colloquially worn out or exhausted.

clue.text: No problem to go around 18 ton transports

definitions.note: plural noun for a singular state

indicators.note: going around something means encircling it, so the first word surrounds what follows

blocks.note: easy means no problem
18 across is TEAR GAS, and CS is the best-known tear gas
T is the abbreviation for ton

explanation.surface: Shifting eighteen tons is said to be no trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transports' looks like haulage but is the noun for rapture, as in transports of delight.
explanation.definitionFit: Transports are overwhelming feelings of joy, so ecstasy, a state of rapture, is the same emotion.

clue.text: Quiet as a spent campanologist on drugs

blocks.note: st! is an old interjection calling for silence, like sh!
a campanologist is a bell-ringer; one who is finished has rung out

explanation.surface: A bell-ringer, exhausted after a long peal, falls silent.
explanation.definitionFit: Strung out is slang for being under the influence of, or addicted to, narcotics.

clue.text: My menu is fantastic, full of this ultimately

definitions.text: My menu is fantastic, full of this ultimately

indicators.note: fantastic means fanciful and unreal, so the letters are freely reimagined in a new order
ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the word is used

blocks.note: taken as written
its final letter

explanation.surface: A chef boasts that every dish on the menu is packed with deliciousness.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue is a chef's boast whose 'this' is the answer itself, so the entire clue is both wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A fantastic menu full of tastiness is one brimming with deliciousness, which is what the noun names.

clue.text: Bit of gyration when on ladder? It's eye-watering stuff

indicators.note: a bit of a word here is just its opening letter
placed on something means coming after it in an across answer, so the earlier pieces go second

blocks.note: a ladder is a run or tear in tights or stockings
its opening letter
as and when both mean at the time that

explanation.surface: A pole dancer's spin on a ladder sounds like a risky, eye-watering stunt.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a ladder is a run in tights.
explanation.definitionFit: Tear gas is a chemical irritant that makes the eyes stream, used to disperse crowds.

clue.text: Maybe inject horse and very old ram outside hospital

indicators.note: being outside something means surrounding it, so the earlier words wrap around the last

blocks.note: so means very, as in so good
O is the abbreviation for old
a tup is a ram, a male sheep
H is the abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: A vet considers injecting a horse and an aged ram outside the animal hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: Horse is slang for heroin, so this is the addict's sense, not the vet's.
explanation.definitionFit: To shoot up is slang for injecting a drug intravenously, and injecting heroin is one example.

clue.text: Republican involved in Times Corporation gaffe

indicators.note: something involved in a matter is caught up inside it, so the letter goes within the word

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican
an era is a period of time
corporation is an old jocular word for a pot belly

explanation.surface: An American politician makes a blunder in a big media company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times Corporation' looks like a media firm; corporation is old British slang for a paunch, here TUM.
explanation.definitionFit: An erratum is an error in printing or writing, so it is a slip or blunder.

clue.text: Those who might guard doors won't open doors

indicators.note: the word cannot open, meaning it loses its opening letter

blocks.note: sentries are posted on watch at gates and entrances

explanation.surface: Guards stationed at doors which stay locked shut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doors' does double duty: it completes the picture of sentries and is the definition itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Entries are ways in, such as doorways or entrances to a building.

clue.text: Violent offender that court banged up

indicators.note: banged up means battered and knocked about, so the letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A thug who was sent to prison by the court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banged up' is British slang for jailed, which suits the surface, but here it scrambles the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A cut-throat is a murderer or ruthless thug, someone who kills by slitting the neck.

clue.text: Something of a tosser?

blocks.note: surface reading: a hint that someone is a bit of an idiot, tosser being British slang
setter's reading: an object belonging to someone who throws things, a log hurled at Highland games

explanation.walkthrough: Tosser is a British insult, but here it means a thrower at Scottish Highland games, and 'of' makes the answer his possession.
explanation.definitionFit: The heavy pole thrown end over end in Scottish athletic contests belongs to the athlete who tosses it.

clue.text: Strike ball heading for net or try a pass?

indicators.note: the heading is the top or front, so the opening letter alone is kept

blocks.note: to strike is to hit
a ball is round like the letter O
its opening letter

explanation.surface: A footballer weighing up whether to shoot at goal or pass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'try a pass' sounds like football, but making a pass at someone is flirting.
explanation.definitionFit: To hit on someone is to make romantic or sexual advances, which is making a pass at them.

clue.text: Banana a fiver? That has saved canteen!

indicators.note: what has been saved is kept inside, so the letters are held within the phrase

blocks.note: letters running across the three words

explanation.surface: Someone is shocked at a pricey banana yet glad the canteen survived.
explanation.walkthrough: The NAAFI runs shops and canteens for the British armed forces.
explanation.definitionFit: The NAAFI is the organisation that runs canteens for British service personnel, so its name is used for such a canteen.

clue.text: Is the setter beginning to get old, mate?

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: the setter asking 'is the setter?' about himself says am I
its opening letter
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: The setter asks a friend whether he is getting on in years.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigo is Spanish for friend and is used in English as a casual word for a pal.

clue.text: Pop singer with Limp Bizkit prefers Britain to Germany

indicators.note: preferring one thing to another means choosing it instead, so one letter is swapped for the other

blocks.note: Fred Durst is the frontman of the American band Limp Bizkit
D is the international vehicle code for Germany
B is an abbreviation for Britain or British

explanation.surface: A rock singer chooses the UK over Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop singer' looks like one phrase; Pop is the definition alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To pop is to burst, as a balloon or bubble breaks open with a bang.

clue.text: Libretto I rewrote for one in rock

indicators.note: rewriting a text recasts it, so the letters are set down in a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lyricist reworks an opera libretto for a rock musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rock' suggests music, but it is stone with a fossil in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Trilobites are extinct marine arthropods now found as fossils embedded in ancient stone.

clue.text: Right bit of trouble with northern element

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
ado is fuss or bother
N is the abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: A spot of bother involving a northern factor.
explanation.definitionFit: Radon is a radioactive noble gas, one of the chemical elements in the periodic table.

clue.text: Silicon found in concoctions for spots

indicators.note: something found in another thing lies inside it, so the element symbol sits within the word

blocks.note: potions are mixed brews
Si is the chemical symbol for silicon

explanation.surface: Silicon is an ingredient in some acne remedies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spots' suggests pimples, matching the potions, but means places.
explanation.definitionFit: Spots and positions are both nouns for particular places or locations where something is situated.
